This page introduces the equations behind `plant` slowly, one idea at a time, for
readers who want to understand the maths but find the
[size-structured PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd) page heavy going. It covers the
same system of equations — just built up gradually, with every symbol explained
in words. Once this feels comfortable, that page has the full derivations,
boundary conditions, and appendices.

If you have not yet read [the big picture](overview.qmd), do that first; this page
puts equations on the concepts introduced there.

## The symbols you will meet

Only a handful of symbols do most of the work. Keep this list nearby:

| Symbol | Means | In words |
|--------|-------|----------|
| $x$ | traits | *what kind* of plant (e.g. its leaf mass per area) |
| $H$ | height | *how big* a plant is — the model's measure of size |
| $a$ | patch age | time since the patch was last cleared by disturbance |
| $E_a$ | light environment | how much light reaches each height in a patch of age $a$ |
| $g,\ d,\ f$ | rates | **g**rowth, **d**eath, and **f**ecundity (seed) rates |
| $N$ | size-density | how many plants of each height are present |
| $P$ | patch-age density | how common patches of each age are |
| $Y_x$ | seed rain | rate at which seeds of strategy $x$ arrive in a patch |

A note on integrals: an integral $\int$ here just means "add up continuously over
time (or over height)." Whenever you see one, read it as a running total.

## Step 1 — one plant, three running totals

Start with a single plant of traits $x$ that germinated at patch age $a_0$. The
strategy gives us its three rates at any moment — growth $g$, death $d$, and
fecundity $f$ — each depending on the plant's current height and the light it
sees. Everything about the individual is a running total of these rates.

**Its height** is its starting height plus all the growth it has accumulated:

$$
H(a) = H_0 + \int_{a_0}^{a} g \, {\rm d}a'.
$$

**Its chance of still being alive** falls off as death accumulates. Survival is
the germination probability times the exponential of *minus* the total death risk
so far:

$$
S_{\rm I}(a) = S_{\rm G} \, \exp\!\left(- \int_{a_0}^{a} d \, {\rm d}a'\right).
$$

The exponential is the standard way to turn a running risk into a survival
probability: no risk yet means survival $1$; as risk piles up, survival decays
towards $0$.

**Its total seeds so far** add up fecundity over time — but only counting plants
that are still alive to produce them, hence the survival factor:

$$
\tilde{R}(a) = \int_{a_0}^{a} f \, S_{\rm I}(a') \, {\rm d}a'.
$$

That is the whole life of one plant: grow, survive, seed — three integrals of the
rates the strategy hands us.

## Step 2 — from one plant to a distribution

A patch holds many plants, so instead of tracking them individually we track a
**size-density distribution** $N(H \mid x, a)$: at patch age $a$, how many plants
of traits $x$ have height $H$. Picture it as a curve over height whose shape
changes as the patch ages.

Two things move that curve, and they map onto the two rates that are *not* about
reproduction:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  G["growth g<br/>pushes plants up<br/>the height axis"] --> N["the size<br/>distribution<br/>N(H | x, a)"]
  D["death d<br/>removes plants<br/>at each height"] --> N
```

Written as an equation, this is the model's central **partial differential
equation (PDE)**:

$$
\frac{\partial N}{\partial a} = \underbrace{-\, d \, N}_{\text{deaths remove plants}} \;\underbrace{-\, \frac{\partial}{\partial H}\big(g \, N\big)}_{\text{growth carries plants upward}}.
$$

Read it as a conveyor belt. Growth $g$ carries plants along the height axis (the
second term is the *flow* of that belt); death $d$ removes a fraction of them
wherever they are (the first term). The left-hand side is simply how the
distribution changes as the patch gets older.

New plants enter at the bottom of the height axis. The rate they enter is set by
how many seeds arrive and how fast the smallest plants grow — this is the PDE's
**boundary condition**, and it is where the seed rain $Y_x$ (Step 4) comes in.

## Step 3 — competition through shade

The rates $g$ and $d$ are not fixed: they depend on light, and light depends on
all the other plants. `plant` uses a shading law borrowed from optics (Beer's
law): light falls off exponentially with the amount of leaf area stacked above
you.

$$
E_a(z) = \exp\!\left(-k_{\rm I} \times (\text{leaf area above height } z)\right).
$$

Here $z$ is a height in the canopy, $E_a(z)$ is the fraction of open-sky light
reaching it, and $k_{\rm I}$ is an extinction coefficient (how strongly leaves
block light). More leaves overhead → smaller $E_a(z)$ → deeper shade below.

This closes the feedback loop from [the big picture](overview.qmd): the
distribution $N$ determines the leaf area, the leaf area sets the light $E_a$, and
the light feeds back into the growth and death rates that reshape $N$.

## Step 4 — patches have ages

Zoom out to the landscape. Disturbances strike patches at random, so at any
moment the landscape contains patches of every age. $P(a)$ describes how common
patches of age $a$ are, and it decays as older patches keep getting knocked back
to age zero:

$$
\frac{{\rm d}P}{{\rm d}a} = -\, d_{\rm P}(a) \, P(a),
$$

where $d_{\rm P}(a)$ is the chance a patch of age $a$ is disturbed. If that chance
is constant, old patches are simply rarer and rarer (an exponential
distribution). `plant`'s default instead lets the disturbance risk *rise* with
age — young patches usually survive, old ones almost never do — which gives a
**Weibull** distribution. Either way, the whole thing is summarised by one
number: $\bar{a}$, the mean interval between disturbances.

## Step 5 — the seed rain must balance

Now the two scales meet. Across the whole landscape, a strategy's total seed
output is found by adding up the seeds made in every patch, weighted by how common
patches of that age are:

$$
Y_x = \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty P(a) \, S_{\rm D} \, f \, N \, {\rm d}H \, {\rm d}a.
$$

The inner integral adds seed production over all plant heights in a patch; the
outer integral averages over patches of all ages; $S_{\rm D}$ is the fraction of
seeds surviving dispersal.

Here is the catch: the seed rain $Y_x$ *feeds the patches* (Step 2's boundary
condition) **and** *comes out of them* (the equation above). At equilibrium the
two must be the same number. Finding that self-consistent value is the central
numerical task in `plant` — a fixed-point solve, exactly the loop drawn in
[the big picture](overview.qmd).

## Step 6 — reading off the answers

Once the patch dynamics and the equilibrium seed rain are known, any quantity you
care about is an average over the size distribution, weighted by how common each
patch age is. Schematically, for some quantity $w$ (density, biomass, mortality…):

$$
\text{landscape average of } w = \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty P(a) \, N \, w \; {\rm d}H \, {\rm d}a.
$$

Total stem density, leaf area, biomass, and the size–density (self-thinning)
relationship all come out of this one weighted-integral pattern — see the
[emergent properties](../guides/emergent-properties.qmd) guide for it in action.
